claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment between 12:46 and 13:07 in which 9.70 km were driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km and straying up to 1720 m from the optimal route; this segment is a route deviation under RD-1 and is not exempted by any RD-3/RD-4/RD-5 ground.

The trip was a RydeTAXI metered trip billed on distance and time ($28.31 for 20.1 km and $8.84 for 34.0 min), so the extra 4.08 km of the unexempted segment entered the fare at the trip's per-km rate of $1.41/km, giving a partial refund of 4.08 × $1.41 = $5.75 (rounded to the cent).
No chat messages exist in the app and there is no record of the rider asking for or agreeing to the detour before it began, so the RD-5 pre-departure consent exception cannot apply.

The driver's defence that he 'followed his GPS' is contradicted by the system records: no traffic incident was recorded near the route, weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain, and the alternative roads showed no severe congestion (PIE and CTE band 7 = 60–69 km/h; Paya Lebar Road band 3 = 20–29 km/h), so RD-4 provides no justification for the 4.08 km excess.

The rider's account shows 5 disputes in the last 90 days with 3 upheld (route: 3), so the 90-day upheld route-dispute count is ≥ 1 and the case triggers an account review flag on the driver under RD-6.
The driver's account shows 640 trips in 90 days with only 1 dispute and 0 upheld, which is relevant context for the account review but does not defeat the GPS record of the unexempted deviation.

weaknesses: The rider's own profile (F14) shows 3 upheld route disputes in 90 days, which the driver can use to argue the rider habitually files route complaints; profile facts cannot decide the case (RD-6) but may colour the account review.

The billed excess distance in the fare record is 4.6 km (F4), while the off-route segment adds only 4.08 km (F3), so the driver/the panel could argue for the larger $6.50 figure or resist refunding the 0.52 km gap; RD-2 limits the refund to the unexempted segment and excludes mapping residual, so we claim $5.75, not $6.50.
No chat exists (F7), so we cannot show the rider objected in-trip; the rider may be seen as having silently acquiesced, though RD-5 requires pre-departure agreement and none is recorded.
The driver's rating is 4.8 with 0 upheld disputes (F15), which may weigh against a finding of deliberate detouring even though RD-1 has no intent requirement.

events.title: Proposed ruling: refund_partial $5.75 (model confidence 0.90)
events.body: The single off-route segment in F3 (12:46–13:07, 9.70 km driven vs 5.62 km optimal, +4.08 km, straying up to 1720 m) is a route deviation under RD-1, and both advocates accept it is the only segment; the driver's statement in F8 that he simply followed his GPS does not create a reasonable cause, and system records (gps/fare) override that bare statement. Nothing about the segment is exempted: F7 shows no chat at all, so there is no pre-departure driver request plus rider agreement for RD-5, and no rider-requested stop for RD-3(a); F12 records no traffic incident near the route, and RD-4(b) alone (band records F9/F10/F11) cannot exempt a segment, so RD-4(a)/(c) route the segment to RD-2.

ruling.recommended_action: Refund $5.75 as a Ryde voucher to the rider for the unexempted 4.08 km off-route segment; no account flag on the driver.
ruling.reasoning: The single off-route segment in F3 (12:46–13:07, 9.70 km driven vs 5.62 km optimal, +4.08 km, straying up to 1720 m) is a route deviation under RD-1, and both advocates accept it is the only segment; the driver's statement in F8 that he simply followed his GPS does not create a reasonable cause, and system records (gps/fare) override that bare statement. Nothing about the segment is exempted: F7 shows no chat at all, so there is no pre-departure driver request plus rider agreement for RD-5, and no rider-requested stop for RD-3(a); F12 records no traffic incident near the route, and RD-4(b) alone (band records F9/F10/F11) cannot exempt a segment, so RD-4(a)/(c) route the segment to RD-2.

rejected_claims.reason: Accepted in outcome but misstated as 'no congestion': F11 shows Paya Lebar Road band 3 (20–29 km/h), i.e. the corridor was not fully clear; exemption still fails because RD-4(a) requires an incident on the replaced optimal stretch (F12 records none) and RD-4(b) band evidence alone does not exempt, so the segment stays non-exempt under RD-4(c).

Fails: RD-6 turns on the driver's own profile route_disputes_upheld_90d ≥ 1, and F15 shows 0 upheld; the rider's 3 upheld route disputes (F14) are another party's profile and profile facts cannot decide or attach the flag here.

Following your GPS doesn't by itself justify that, and records show no rider agreement to the detour, no requested stop, and no traffic incident on that stretch. So $5.75 of the fare is being refunded to the rider as a Ryde voucher. No penalty or account flag applies to you, and no action is needed on your side.

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment between 12:46 and 13:07 in which 9.70 km were driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km and straying up to 1720 m from the optimal route; this segment is a route deviation under RD-1 and is not exempted by any RD-3/RD-4/RD-5 ground.

The trip was a RydeTAXI metered trip billed on distance and time ($28.31 for 20.1 km and $8.84 for 34.0 min), so the extra 4.08 km of the unexempted segment entered the fare at the trip's per-km rate of $1.41/km, giving a partial refund of 4.08 × $1.41 = $5.75 (rounded to the cent).
No chat messages exist in the app and there is no record of the rider asking for or agreeing to the detour before it began, so the RD-5 pre-departure consent exception cannot apply.

The driver's defence that he 'followed his GPS' is contradicted by the system records: no traffic incident was recorded near the route, weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain, and the alternative roads showed no severe congestion (PIE and CTE band 7 = 60–69 km/h; Paya Lebar Road band 3 = 20–29 km/h), so RD-4 provides no justification for the 4.08 km excess.

The rider's account shows 5 disputes in the last 90 days with 3 upheld (route: 3), so the 90-day upheld route-dispute count is ≥ 1 and the case triggers an account review flag on the driver under RD-6.
The driver's account shows 640 trips in 90 days with only 1 dispute and 0 upheld, which is relevant context for the account review but does not defeat the GPS record of the unexempted deviation.

weaknesses: The rider's own profile (F14) shows 3 upheld route disputes in 90 days, which the driver can use to argue the rider habitually files route complaints; profile facts cannot decide the case (RD-6) but may colour the account review.

The billed excess distance in the fare record is 4.6 km (F4), while the off-route segment adds only 4.08 km (F3), so the driver/the panel could argue for the larger $6.50 figure or resist refunding the 0.52 km gap; RD-2 limits the refund to the unexempted segment and excludes mapping residual, so we claim $5.75, not $6.50.
No chat exists (F7), so we cannot show the rider objected in-trip; the rider may be seen as having silently acquiesced, though RD-5 requires pre-departure agreement and none is recorded.
The driver's rating is 4.8 with 0 upheld disputes (F15), which may weigh against a finding of deliberate detouring even though RD-1 has no intent requirement.

claims.assertion: The only off-route segment on the record is a single stretch from 12:46 to 13:07 in which 9.70 km was driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km; this is the sole deviation the RD-2 calculation may be built on.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (total $42.52 with a per-km distance component of $28.31 for 20.1 km), so any refund is confined to the metered distance units of the unexempted segment at the trip's per-km rate, not to the whole fare.

The rider's own estimate of 'about 15 km' against 'almost 20 km' matches the GPS record of 20.1 km actual vs 15.5 km optimal, so the distance complaint is grounded in the system record and cannot be dismissed as a perception issue — but it also means the refund is bounded by the measured 4.08 km segment, not the raw 4.6 km total.

The driver cannot claim a reroute justified by congestion: the only speed-band records are band 7 (60–69 km/h) on CTE and PIE and band 3 (20–29 km/h) on Paya Lebar Road, and there is no incident record near the route — so neither RD-4(a) nor RD-4(b) exempts the segment.

The driver's statement that he 'followed my GPS' and that 'nothing wrong with the fare' is uncorroborated: there is no in-app chat at all, so nothing shows the rider agreed to the Paya Lebar exit before the vehicle left the optimal route.

The driver's clean 90-day record (640 trips, 1 dispute, 0 upheld, rating 4.8) supports treating this deviation as a one-off navigation error rather than a repeated pattern, so no flag_account is warranted under RD-6.

The rider's profile (5 disputes in 90 days, 3 upheld, all route-related) shows an active dispute pattern, which supports weighing the complaint strictly against the measured segment rather than the rider's framing.

weaknesses: The GPS record squarely contradicts the driver's position: F1 shows 20.1 km actual vs 15.5 km optimal (+30%) and F3 isolates a 4.08 km unexplained off-route segment, which the rider's counsel will use to establish an unexempted deviation under RD-1/RD-2 and demand at least 4.08 km of metered distance back.

The driver's statement in F8 ('I followed my GPS, nothing wrong with the fare') is a bare statement that conflicts with the GPS facts (F1, F3) and loses to them; it also gives no reasonable cause, and F12 confirms there was no traffic incident that could exempt the segment under RD-4(a).
There is no chat agreement in F7 to invoke RD-5, so the driver has no consent defence for the route change even though the rider's own profile in F14 shows 3 previously upheld route disputes.
F2 (34.0 min vs 22 min estimated, +12.2 min) shows the deviation also cost time, which the rider will cite to argue the detour was not even an efficiency choice.

points.response: Accepted: we build our refund solely on the single off-route segment F3 identifies (9.70 km driven vs 5.62 km optimal, +4.08 km), so the driver's own reading of RD-1 supports rather than opposes a finding of unexempted deviation.

Agreed on the RydeTAXI metering method (F6), and that is exactly our claim: 4.08 km × the trip's per-km rate of $1.41/km (F4: $28.31 ÷ 20.1 km) = $5.75, not the whole fare — the driver concedes the refund formula, leaving only the amount to be ordered.

The driver's own concession that the complaint is grounded in the system record (F1: 20.1 km actual vs 15.5 km optimal; F3: 4.08 km unexempted segment) establishes the deviation liability; the bounding point is already reflected in our $5.75 figure, which excludes the 0.52 km mapping residual in F4's 4.6 km.

This concession is decisive: with no incident record near the route (F12) and only band 7 (60–69 km/h) on CTE/PIE and band 3 (20–29 km/h) on Paya Lebar Road (F9, F10, F11), plus fair weather (F13), no RD-4 exemption can save the segment, so RD-2 applies and $5.75 must be refunded.

The driver admits there is no chat evidence (F7) and his bare statement (F8) loses to the GPS facts; RD-5 therefore cannot exempt the segment, and the deviation stands unexempted for the full 4.08 km.

Contested: RD-6 attaches flag_account on the account state of the party against whom the deviation is established (rider profile F14 shows 3 upheld route disputes in 90 days, making this incident part of a repeated record), and the driver's own trip count (F15) does not displace that counter — profile facts only drive the additional action, never the liability finding.
Contested: F14 is a profile fact and cannot decide the case either way under RD-6; the finding rests on F1 and F3, which the driver does not dispute.

We do not contest that a single off-route segment exists (F3: 12:46–13:07, 9.70 km vs 5.62 km, +4.08 km), but RD-1's obligation is judged per segment and the record shows exactly one segment, so nothing beyond it may be treated as a deviation.

The rider's arithmetic over-extracts: RD-2 refunds only the unexempted segment's extra_km at the per-km rate, and the trip's own fare record already quantifies the refundable excess as 4.6 km × $1.41 = $6.50 (F4) against a distance charge of $28.31 for 20.1 km (F6), so the segment-derived 4.08 km gives $5.75 and the 0.52 km gap is mapping residual that RD-2 expressly leaves unrefunded.

There being no chat at all (F7) cuts both ways — it equally gives the rider no in-trip objection, and the rider's complaint itself states no route request was made, so the Paya Lebar exit was a navigation choice, not a granted request under RD-3(a).

The traffic record actually undercuts the claim that the driver had no reason to leave the PIE: the optimal corridor is not shown clear of slowing (F10 PIE band 7 only until 12:46, F11 Paya Lebar Road band 3 through 13:15), yet because RD-4 requires an incident within 300 m of the replaced route and F12 records none, we accept the segment is not exempted.

RD-6 cannot be satisfied by the rider's own history: the clause requires the DRIVER's profile to show route_disputes_upheld_90d ≥ 1, and F15 shows the driver at 0 upheld disputes, while F14's 3 upheld route disputes belong to the rider and profile facts may never decide the case.
We adopt this: the driver's 640 trips in 90 days with 1 dispute and 0 upheld and a 4.8 rating (F15) is the record RD-6 actually looks at, and it confirms no account flag is triggered.
